pitch_detail.notes: Start well right of the couloir's foot: the slabs straight below it carry patchy ice. The rock is compact and runout, with little natural protection — knifeblades and angles are what hold. Parties simul-climb it; in winter it is thin ice and hard névé over rock. Build the last belay beneath an overhang just below the snowfield.

Turn the corner onto the big snowfield and traverse left toward the couloir entrance. The slope steepens at its left end and hangs directly above the lower rock band, with the glacier roughly 1,000 ft below — a slip here would not stop. Anchors are poor; expect to combine a cam, a short screw and a horn.

Two belayed leads. A vertical snow-ice strip on the left does not reach the couloir; go right instead, across a partly iced slab and over a rock bulge into the corner under a big chockstone, where the belay is good. The second lead climbs a fragile snow tongue to the chockstone and passes it on steep ice on the left, with a cam under the roof. The right-hand ice is hollow.

Above the chockstone the couloir runs long and very exposed. A rib along one side of the scoured runnel gives the line; simul-climb and move fast, because the cornices hang over it. It tops out on the summit ridge near 6,700 ft. The summit is still about an hour along the ridge, and south-side snow turns to mush in sun. Parties often rappel from pitons onto the SE ridge instead.

review.changed: Same four sections, same labels. Lower band graded 5.6 (the lower pitches are called 5.6 in summer); the stored 'mid-5th' is dropped. The notes now say where to start (right of the iced slabs), what the protection is (pitons), what the snowfield exposure and anchors are like, the two crux leads (slab and corner, then the chockstone with its snow tongue and the good left-side ice), and the upper couloir's rib, cornices and top-out. No grade or crux flag on the crux pitches: no source gives a summer grade for them. No lengths anywhere. Pitch detail comes from one detailed first-winter-ascent report, backed by the AAJ summary (difficult mixed climbing low in the couloir, straightforward snow above), so medium confidence at most. The notes describe winter conditions where they differ.
review.other_findings: The FA year is uncertain. The stored fa says July 1974 or 1976; a peak page gives 1972 for Kloke and Simon. The AAJ dates the first winter ascent to March 13, 2005, and the trip report is headed 3/12/2005 (the stored fa has March 13). descent_text quotes a climber ('The 2005 party's words: ...') and rappels quotes a report. Both are testimony and credit a party, so a human should reword them.

pitch_detail.notes: Hannegan Pass trail into the Chilliwack valley, ford the river, then the old Easy Ridge path to Easy Saddle and along the crest over Easy Peak. Short of Whatcom, the Imperfect Impasse gully blocks the ridge. Its high crossing is exposed and hard to find, so many parties drop to about 4,400 ft to cross it safely, then climb back up to camp at Perfect Pass (about 6,200 ft).

Head north from Perfect Pass up the broad, moderate snowfield on the south side, aiming for the obvious col in the summit ridge. It is the margin of the Whatcom Glacier: treat it as glacier travel early in the season, and watch for moats opening against the rock later in summer. It takes about an hour from camp, and on good snow it makes a fast descent.

Get onto the crest at the col, or by ramps and ledges just northeast of it, and follow the narrow south ridge to the top. Grades from 3rd to 4th class are given. The moves are moderate, but the drop is big on both sides and the rock is poor, so many parties rope up and place a few pieces. The northeast of the two summit points is higher: the right-hand one as seen from Perfect Pass.

review.changed: Same three sections and labels. The approach notes now say how to get past the Imperfect Impasse. The snowfield notes cover the glacier margin, moats and timing. The summit ridge notes give the exposure, rock quality, roping practice and which summit is higher. Its chip was 'Class 4, poor rock' and is now 'Class 3–4', because recent reports call the crest Class 3. The stored '~100 ft' is dropped from the notes. No lengths.
review.other_findings: The stored route grade '4th' is on the high side: three recent trip reports call the summit ridge Class 3 (one says Class 2+ on descent), with 4th class coming from the older guidebook grading. climbing_route step 3 says the crest is 'on the order of a hundred feet'; that figure could not be confirmed.

pitch_detail.notes: From the Cinderella–Little Sister col, stay close to the crest of the jagged southeast ridge. The climbing is easy low fifth class, but exposed the whole way, on grippy, solid dunite that takes gear well; a light alpine rack is enough. The ridge is longer than it looks, with several false summits.

Higher up the ridge widens and the rock gets looser. Pick a way through 4th-class blocks and ledges to the true summit, testing holds and keeping the rope out of loose rubble. To descend, downclimb the ridge (a south-facing gully leads off it to easier ground) or rappel the North Face on scattered old pin and tat anchors.

review.changed: Three rows become two, deliberately. The only route description says 3 pitches and 700 ft, but never divides the ground into pitches. The stored table did: it gave P1 the route grade 5.3, gave P2 an invented '5.0-5.2', and split the route length evenly (70/71/71 m). All of those numbers are dropped. The two remaining sections are the two kinds of ground the description names: the low-5th crest, then 4th class above. There are no lengths and no per-pitch grades. P1/P2/P3 comments, if any exist, will not carry over. Single primary source plus one circuit trip report, so medium.
review.other_findings: The stored lengthM values (70/71/71) look back-filled from length_m 213 ÷ 3, and no source gives pitch lengths. pitches=3 and length_m=213 match the route description (3 pitches, 700 ft). The area page gives Little Sister's elevation as 6,017 ft, but a Mountaineers page says 6,600 ft. Check the stored summit elevation.

pitch_detail.notes: Start up either of the two clean corners on the west side of the ridge, south of the peak; they reach the crest in about half a pitch. From the crest, move right on chickenheads and face holds. Above the corner the face can be coated in black lichen, with poor protection, and a solid anchor on the choss of the crest is hard to find. Carry slings and small gear for it.

A short pitch across the Cannon Hole, a natural arch between two small towers that formed in a rockfall in the 1980s or 1990s. The crossing opens with an exposed lean from a knife edge onto the rock of the arch, then traverses over it. The rock around the arch looks unstable, so move gently.

It is given as low fifth class to the summit, but the line is not obvious: going both high and low tends to dead-end near a notch with old tat. One way through is a delicate, very exposed stem around a corner (graded 5.8–5.9) and a downclimb into the notch, then dirty low-fifth ground to the top. A follower on that step risks a pendulum, so consider rappelling it off the tat.

review.changed: Same three pitches and labels. P3's grade token is fixed from '5th class (low)' to 'low 5th'. P1 now warns about the black lichen and the hard-to-find anchor. P2 describes the knife-edge move onto the Cannon Hole and how the arch formed. P3 warns about the route-finding dead-end and the exposed step, with its 5.8–5.9 grade, and the follower pendulum. No crux flag, bolts or lengths: no source states them for a pitch. The one length reported (45 m for P1) was found to be well over the real length, so it is left out. Confidence is medium because it rests on one route description and one detailed 2025 report, with a third source confirming three short pitches on marginal rock.
review.other_findings: The stored discipline is 'mountaineering', but this is a 3-pitch trad alpine rock route (Grade II, 5.8), so 'alpine' fits better. The recent report calls the route poor-quality rock throughout and found P3's 'low 5th' needing a 5.8–5.9 step. The stored overview's 'clean granite climbing' is contradicted: it should be 'marginal rock'. The approach column says the standard approach is from Downey Creek via the Ptarmigan Traverse, while the route description says the corners are approached from Blue Lake. A human should look at both.

wa_mount_degenhardt_southwest_route.skip_reason: The row mixes two climbs and its identity is unclear. It is named 'Southwest Route'. Its pitch_detail and beta describe the line from Crescent Creek Basin to the summit horn, which one trip report calls the 'Corkscrew Route' (Class 4 slot to the north ridge, Class 4-5 face to the west ridge, Class 3 ledge to the south ridge); descent_text also follows that line. climbing_route instead describes a different line: up choss to the notch south of the summit (the upper Barrier crossing), then the south ridge, which is what other sources call the South Route. The 'Southwest Route' name could not be matched to either line in any source found, so neither was picked. Research found: the South Route (via the Barrier notch) is 4th class to low 5th, and traversing too low puts parties on roped 5.7 ground. On the Corkscrew line, a single rappel or downclimb is used from the summit step.

pitch_detail.notes: Kick up the snow finger that runs up between the main and south spires on the west face, and step onto rock where the snow is breached — check the moat there. A short wall leads to a broad ledge. From the ledge the route trends left.

Traverse left from the ledge to a steep corner of black rock and climb it. The final 15 ft or so are the route's technical crux: exposed 5.6 moves on solid granite. Remember where the top of this corner is: the second descent rappel ends here, and the last person down places a directional to keep the rope running true.

Keep going left on Class 3 granite into a conspicuous dike of reddish-black basalt, and follow it up to the high notch between the main and north spires. The dike is easy but somewhat loose: keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line.

A vertical headwall blocks any direct exit from the notch. Downclimb about 20 ft, then traverse right across steep but solid, well-broken rock to a shallow gully running parallel to the dike. This is where parties lose the line, and working it out can cost hours.

Climb the shallow gully by a string of short chimneys and cracks, the hardest around 5.5, to the ridge crest. You reach the crest at a large horn draped in rappel slings, about 50 ft below the top. It confirms you are on route, and it is the anchor for the first double-rope rappel down the West Face.

Follow the narrow crest over large, solid granite blocks. It is wildly exposed, with moves from Class 3 to low fifth. The true summit is a tiny horn about the size of a barstool, and climbers usually take turns on it. Reverse the crest, belayed, back to the slung horn to descend.

review.changed: Same six sections and labels. The start is now placed: the snow finger between the main and south spires, a breach, and a moat. The dike is flagged as loose, the notch as a route-finding time sink, and the horn as the rappel anchor. The summit grade token is fixed from 'Class 3 (low 5th)' to 'low 5th'. Crux flag added to the black dihedral: the source calls its top 15 ft the technical crux of the route. Two unsourced chips are removed: 'Class 3-4' on the lower wall and 'Class 4' on the notch traverse, which the source gives no class for. Both are now plain terrain descriptions. All the ascent detail traces to one trip report (reposted on a second site), so medium; the descent details come from the stored descent_text.
review.other_findings: The grade 'Class 5.6 / glacier' is not a clean grade value. Other parties describe a different line on the same summit as 'the classic SW (Beckey) route': about 5 short pitches of low to mid 5th on knobby rock, starting from a small cave above the moat. Whether this 'Standard Route' is that line or the dike-and-notch line in the table is not settled by any source. A human may want to confirm the row's name. The overview says 'Chikamin Glacier to the west and Blue Glacier to the east'; that is correct.

wa_robinson_mountain_north_couloir.skip_reason: No pitch-level (or any) description of a North Couloir on Robinson Mountain was found. The peak page, three trip reports and several searches mention only the Southeast Ridge standard route and an east-face couloir. The stored lengthM values (91 + 305 + 30 m) add up exactly to length_m 427 and look back-filled. The angle ranges (30-35°, 40-50°) have no traceable source either. A human should consider whether this row's existing table can be trusted.
